cards.text: This is a psalm of David, king of Israel, and friend, it's short but it is LOADED. David tells us what the LORD said to someone David calls my Lord. Lean in, because this is one conversation you do NOT want to miss.

cards.question: The LORD speaks to the one David calls my Lord. What does the LORD tell Him to do?

answers.text: Go out ahead of My army

cards.question: The LORD tells David's Lord to sit there until His enemies come and make peace with Him.

cards.text: His enemies, made a footstool for His feet. And friend, I know footstool life, because in that junk drawer takeout menus sat on ME for YEARS.

Centuries later, Jesus asks the Pharisees, the religious leaders, whose son the Christ is, and they say David's. So Jesus points them right to this line and asks how David can call Him Lord (Matthew 22:41-45).

cards.question: Next, the LORD extends the mighty scepter of David's Lord. Where does it reach out from?
With that scepter in hand, the LORD tells David's Lord to wait until every enemy is gone before He starts to rule.

cards.text: Not after the enemies are gone, but right there “in the midst of Your enemies.” Then David turns to His people on His day of battle.

cards.question: On the day of battle for David's Lord, His people shall be ___.

cards.text: WILLING, friend, and that is HUGE, because you ask the group chat who can help move a couch and suddenly everybody's phone is dead. Then David paints it in big pictures: holy splendor, the womb of the dawn, the dew of Your youth.
Now the LORD makes an oath, and He will not change His mind. Me? I change my mind about toppings forty times a batch, so that line right there is humbling.

cards.question: The LORD swears an oath to David's Lord. What does He swear this Lord will be?
The LORD swore this and will not change His mind. What does that tell you about this promise?

answers.text: It lasts until the next king

cards.question: This priesthood is in the order of Melchizedek. In Genesis 14 he meets Abram after a battle, and he's king of Salem and ___ of God Most High.

cards.text: And the book of Hebrews connects it for us: Jesus has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 6:20).
Then the picture flips. Back in verse 1 He was told to sit at the LORD's right hand, and now David says the Lord is at Your right hand.

cards.question: The Lord is at His right hand, and He will crush ___ in the day of His wrath.
In this day of wrath, His judgment stays inside Israel's borders.

cards.text: He will judge the nations, heaping up the dead, and crush the leaders far and wide. Then the psalm ends on a quiet picture: He drinks from the brook by the road.

cards.question: In the psalm's last line, He drinks from the brook by the road. What does He do because of it?

findings.problem: The question says 'sit there' and uses 'His enemies' and 'Him'. These point back to the right hand from card 2, which is no longer on screen. The question doesn't say where 'there' is.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: 'With that scepter in hand' points back to the scepter in card 6's question, which the baker can no longer see.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The blank is the next word of the psalm's line: 'Your people shall be ___.' The baker has to guess the wording of a line they haven't seen. They aren't reasoning out its meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: 'Then the picture flips' says that verse 5 reverses verse 1. That decides who 'the Lord' is and who 'Your' is in verse 5, and the text leaves both open. The card should tell what verse 5 says without deciding who is at whose right hand.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The blank is the next word of verse 5's line: 'He will crush ___ in the day of His wrath.' The baker has to guess unseen wording. Nothing on the earlier cards lets them reason it out.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The question asks the baker to finish the psalm's last line ('therefore He will lift up His head'). Nothing earlier lets them reason it out. This is the same as the Psalm 23 'paths of…' bad example.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: Cards 5 (Matthew 22:41-45) and 15 (Hebrews 6:20) are whole story cards about New Testament passages. They don't tell any part of Psalm 110. They also use those passages to name the psalm's 'my Lord' and priest as Jesus. The docs allow outside facts 'when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter.' They also say 'Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.' They don't say whether New Testament fulfillment cards like these belong in Prep, or whether they should be left for the Big Idea.
findings.question: Can Prep give whole story cards to New Testament passages that quote or explain the passage, and use them to name who an unnamed figure in the psalm is? Or should Prep stay inside the passage and leave that to the Big Idea?
